newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Violence, crime choke South African tourism.
newsitem.headline: Violence, crime choke South African tourism.

text.p: On a recent summer Sunday, a riot broke out in Cape Town's premier tourist spot -- the Victoria and Alfred Waterfront at the foot of Table Mountain.
As hundreds of vacationers looked on, a protester aligned with a militant Moslem movement opposed to drugs was killed and scores of demonstrators were injured in skirmishes with police.
The Moslem group, People Against Gangsterism and Drugs, had burst into the limelight in August when members publicly shot and burned to death an alleged drug merchant and gang leader.

The recent clash would have been less surprising if it had happened in Johannesburg, South Africa's financial capital, where violent crime is rampant. But Cape Town, the political centre, is widely viewed as by far the safer of the two cities.
Blaming burgeoning crime and violence, South Africa's tourism industry says the number of foreign visitors this summer will be disappointing due to worries about personal safety.
The South African Tourism Board (Satour) forecasts a rise of only 10 percent during the October-January summer season, compared with a 22 percent jump in the same period last year.
Violent crime is the main reason, analysts say.
South Africa took off as a tourist destination shortly after its first democratic elections in April 1994, which ended its years of isolation due to apartheid and political unrest.
Its attractiveness soared when it hosted the 1995 World Cup Rugby tournament.
But lately, gruesome tales of crime and violence splashed across newspapers and television screens around the world have spooked potential tourists and given an edge to other countries.
"Crime is still deterring tourists. Our competitors play on our bad points, like crime," Roger Mackie, president of the Association of South African Travel Agents (ASATA), told Reuters.

"We hear politicians saying that we are no worse than anywhere in the world, but we are. You can walk around Sydney harbour anytime at night and not get shot. You cannot do it here. Crime has to be brought down to acceptable levels."
A total of 1.98 million serious crimes was reported last year, only half of them solved, including 36,888 rapes, 18,983 murders and 66,838 armed robberies.
Many, weary of being victims, have taken the law into their own hands and in a vicious circle, crime triggers violent retaliation such as the riot at Cape Town's waterfront.

Forecasting approximately 450,000 foreign vacationers this summer compared with 410,000 last summer, James Seymour, head of Satour's information management and research division, told Reuters: "We could definitely have done better."
Industry analysts dismissed any hopes of a tourism boom in the near future, saying the country's scenery and wildlife was losing the battle to armed robbery, rape and murder.

"We saw a boom last year which seems to have cooled off a bit and, considering the crime levels, I'm not sure there is any real good reason for it to start up again," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Not even the South African rand's dramatic decline against key currencies -- offering value-for-money vacations to overseas travelers -- seems able to offset fears for personal safety.
"Tourists should be coming here in their hordes because of our rate of exchange. But they're not," an analyst said.
Satour's Seymour believes the industry will see better days. "The potential to grow at a rate of 20 percent per annum is definitely there," he said.
But he said that in addition to promising tourist safety, the industry should market itself better and ensure competitive pricing and adequate services.
Desperate to keep the tourists coming, the industry is demanding a quick fix such as high-profile policing.
"There is no real short-term solution as such, but it's really visibility, high-profile policing and improving the perception," Seymour said.
But others argue that giant armoured vehicles cruising seaside streets and armed police on every corner might be more off-putting than confidence-inspiring.
